processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea. It is suited to black tea, so the usual path is the standard one for that class: withering, rolling, oxidation and drying.
harvest_season: Little is recorded for this cultivar in particular. It is a mid-season variety, and as with other Chinese black teas, spring pickings are usually the most valued.
appearance_dry: Varies with the maker; as with other large-leaf black teas, expect dark, fairly sturdy twisted leaf.
appearance_liquor: As is typical of black tea from large-leaf plants, a clear reddish amber.
appearance_wet: The growing plant has elliptic green leaves; as with other large-leaf black teas, the steeped leaf turns coppery brown.
taste_profile: No tasting record specific to this cultivar is well established. Black teas from large-leaf plants typically give a malty, brisk cup with some sweetness.

brewing.notes: General guidance for large-leaf black tea, not specific to this cultivar: start short, since this type of leaf can turn astringent, and lengthen from there.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under its own name. Its leaf normally goes into regional black teas, sold like other Chinese black tea by the current year's harvest and best drunk within a couple of years.
description:
Qianmei 502 is a tea plant, not a tea you will usually see on a shelf. It is a clonal, large-leaf, mid-season cultivar bred in Guizhou and recognised at national level in China, and it is also known as Nanbeihong.

Its parents explain its purpose: Fengqing large-leaf from Yunnan brought quality, and the cold-hardy Xuan'en long-leaf brought resilience. The result is a small tree with an open habit, and it is regarded as a black tea plant.

Few tasting notes name this cultivar directly, so treat any cup as what is typical of large-leaf black teas: malty and brisk, with sweetness if handled gently. Short first steeps are the safe approach.

It grows mainly in southern and southwestern Guizhou and has been introduced to Sichuan, Chongqing, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hunan and Fujian. If a seller names it, ask who made the tea and which harvest it is, because the cultivar alone tells you little about the cup.
history:
The Meitan tea research institute in Guizhou, now the Guizhou Tea Research Institute, bred it between 1958 and 1965 by crossing Fengqing large-leaf as the mother with Xuan'en long-leaf as the father.

In 1987 the national crop variety committee recognised it as a national variety, number GS13002-1987.
